questions.q: Zinc is in the d-block but is not a transition metal. Why?

options.A: Its only ion, \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), has a completely filled d sub-shell.
options.B: Its only ion, \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), has no d electrons at all.
options.C: Zinc atoms have no electrons in the 4s sub-shell.
options.D: Zinc does not form any compounds with a variable oxidation state because it is too unreactive.

questions.solution: A transition metal forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. Zinc forms only \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}}\), whose d sub-shell is full. (An empty d sub-shell is the reason scandium is excluded: \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(\mathrm{[Ar]}\).)

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of the \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) ion? (Fe: Z = 26)
questions.solution: Iron is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{6}\,4s^{2}}\). The 4s electrons are lost first, then one 3d electron, so \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{5}}\). (Removing the three electrons from the 3d sub-shell first is the common slip, leaving \(\mathrm{3d^{3}\,4s^{2}}\).)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why transition metals show variable oxidation numbers?

options.A: Ligands split the d orbitals into two sets of different energy.
options.B: Transition metals have very high first ionisation energies, so they never lose all their outer electrons.
options.C: The 3d electrons are always lost before the 4s electrons.
options.D: The 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies, so different numbers of them can be lost or used in bonding.

questions.solution: Because the 4s and 3d sub-shells are close in energy, removing one more electron costs only a little more energy, which can be recovered from bonding or hydration. So several oxidation states are stable. (d-orbital splitting explains colour, not variable oxidation number; and the 4s electrons are lost first.)

questions.q: How is each water ligand bonded to the metal ion in \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\)?

options.A: By a co-ordinate bond: the \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ion donates a pair of electrons to the oxygen atom.
options.B: By a co-ordinate bond: the oxygen atom donates a lone pair of electrons to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\).
options.C: By an ionic bond between \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) and the \(\delta-\) oxygen atom.
options.D: By a hydrogen bond from a hydrogen atom of the water to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\).

questions.solution: A ligand is an electron-pair donor. Each water molecule uses one lone pair on its oxygen atom to form a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond to the metal ion, which accepts the pair. (Hydrogen atoms in water have no lone pairs to donate.)

questions.q: What are the oxidation state of cobalt and the co-ordination number in \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2})_{2}Cl_{2}]^{+}}\)?

options.D: +3 and 6

questions.solution: 1,2-diaminoethane is neutral and each chloride is −1, so Co − 2 = +1 and cobalt is +3. Each 1,2-diaminoethane is bidentate, forming two co-ordinate bonds, so the co-ordination number is 2 × 2 + 2 = 6. (Counting ligands, not bonds, leads to 4.)

questions.q: What is the shape of the \(\mathrm{[CuCl_{4}]^{2-}}\) ion, and its bond angle?

options.D: Linear, 180°

questions.solution: Chloride ions are large, so only four fit around \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). Four bonding pairs repel as far apart as possible, giving a tetrahedral ion with bond angles of 109.5°. (Square planar four-co-ordinate complexes such as cisplatin are the exception, not the rule, for chloride.)

questions.q: Cisplatin, \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]}\), is used to treat cancer. Which describes its structure?

options.A: Square planar, with the two chloride ligands opposite each other, at 180°
options.B: Tetrahedral, with the two chloride ligands next to each other
options.C: Octahedral, with the two chloride ligands next to each other
options.D: Square planar, with the two chloride ligands next to each other, at 90° to each other

questions.solution: Cisplatin is a square planar complex, and "cis" means the two chloride ligands are on the same side, at 90°. Only this isomer can bind to DNA in the way that stops cancer cells dividing, so it is supplied pure, without the trans isomer. (A tetrahedral complex cannot have cis and trans forms.)

questions.q: Which type of stereoisomerism is shown by \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2})_{3}]^{2+}}\)?

options.D: No stereoisomerism, because all three ligands are the same

questions.solution: Three bidentate ligands wrap around the octahedral nickel ion like a propeller, in either a left-handed or a right-handed sense. The two forms are non-superimposable mirror images, so the complex shows optical isomerism. With three identical bidentate ligands there is no cis–trans arrangement.

questions.q: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to a solution containing \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\). Which shows the cobalt complex formed and the colour change?

options.D: \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{4}Cl_{2}]}\); pink to green

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 4Cl^{-} \rightleftharpoons [CoCl_{4}]^{2-} + 6H_{2}O}\). Chloride ligands are larger than water, so only four fit: the co-ordination number falls from 6 to 4 and the shape changes from octahedral to tetrahedral. The solution turns from pink to blue.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + EDTA^{4-} \rightarrow [Cu(EDTA)]^{2-} + 6H_{2}O}\) is very favourable?

options.A: The bonds from EDTA to copper are much stronger than those from water, so \(\Delta H\) is very negative.
options.B: The number of particles rises from 2 to 7, so \(\Delta S\) is large and positive, while \(\Delta H\) is close to zero.
options.C: The number of particles falls, so \(\Delta S\) is negative but \(\Delta H\) is very negative.
options.D: The EDTA ion has a 4− charge, so it attracts the copper ion much more strongly than water does.

questions.solution: Six Cu–O bonds are broken and six similar co-ordinate bonds to N and O atoms are made, so \(\Delta H\) is near zero. But one EDTA ion releases six water molecules, so the number of particles rises from 2 to 7 and \(\Delta S\) is large and positive. This makes \(\Delta G\) negative: the chelate effect.

questions.q: For a ligand substitution in which a hexadentate ligand replaces six water ligands, \(\Delta H = -3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +180\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). What is \(\Delta G\) at 298 K?
questions.solution: Convert \(\Delta S\) to kJ: 0.180 \(\text{kJ K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) = −3 − (298 × 0.180) = −3 − 53.6 = \(-56.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Not converting J to kJ leads to −53 600.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why a solution of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) ions is blue?

options.A: The ligands split the d orbitals; d electrons absorb blue light to move to the higher level, so blue is seen.
options.B: Electrons are excited by heat and fall back to lower d orbitals, emitting blue light.
options.C: The ligands split the d orbitals; d electrons absorb light in the red-orange region to move to the higher level, and the blue light that is not absorbed is transmitted.
options.D: The 4s electrons absorb visible light and move into the empty 3d orbitals.

questions.solution: Water ligands split the 3d orbitals into two levels separated by \(\Delta E\). A d electron absorbs a photon whose energy equals \(\Delta E\); for this ion that is red-orange light. The remaining wavelengths, mainly blue, are transmitted, so the solution looks blue. (A solution shows the colour it does not absorb.)

questions.q: A complex ion absorbs light of wavelength 620 nm. What is the energy gap between its split d orbitals, per ion? (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\); \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Convert the wavelength: 620 nm = \(6.20 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\). \(\Delta E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{6.20 \times 10^{-7}}\) = \(3.21 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). (Leaving the wavelength in nm leads to \(3.21 \times 10^{-28}\).)

questions.q: Which aqueous ion is colourless?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^{10}}\): every d orbital is full, so no electron can move from the lower to the upper level and no visible light is absorbed. The other ions have partly filled d sub-shells and are coloured: blue, pale green and pink.

questions.q: Zinc and acid reduce vanadium(V) step by step. What colour is the solution when the vanadium is in the +3 oxidation state?

options.D: Green

questions.solution: +5 (\(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}}\)) yellow; +4 (\(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\)) blue; +3 (\(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\)) green; +2 (\(\mathrm{V^{2+}}\)) violet. (A green colour is also seen briefly between yellow and blue, but that is a mixture of +5 and +4.)

questions.q: Use these standard electrode potentials. \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+} + 2H^{+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons VO^{2+} + H_{2}O}\), +1.00 V; \(\mathrm{VO^{2+} + 2H^{+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons V^{3+} + H_{2}O}\), +0.34 V; \(\mathrm{V^{3+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons V^{2+}}\), −0.26 V; \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}\), +0.77 V. Excess \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions are added to acidified \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}}\). What is the final vanadium species?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) can reduce a species whose couple has a more positive \(E^{\ominus}\) than +0.77 V. \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}/VO^{2+}}\) (+1.00 V) qualifies, \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) = +0.23 V. \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}/V^{3+}}\) (+0.34 V) does not, \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) = −0.43 V. So the reduction stops at \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\).

questions.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of an \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) solution reacts with 21.60 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) acidified potassium manganate(VII). What is the concentration of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\)?
How does vanadium(V) oxide act as a catalyst in the Contact process, \(\mathrm{2SO_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2SO_{3}}\)?

options.A: \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\) reduces \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) and is oxidised to \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{6}}\), which then reacts with \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\).
options.B: \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\) adsorbs \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) on its surface without any change in the oxidation state of vanadium.
options.C: \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\) oxidises \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) to \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) and is reduced to \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{4}}\), which oxygen then oxidises back to \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\).
options.D: \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\) dissolves in the gas mixture and acts as a homogeneous catalyst.

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{SO_{2} + V_{2}O_{5} \rightarrow SO_{3} + V_{2}O_{4}}\), then \(\mathrm{2V_{2}O_{4} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2V_{2}O_{5}}\). Vanadium goes from +5 to +4 and back, so the catalyst is regenerated. Its ability to change oxidation state is what makes it work. (It is a solid with gaseous reactants, so it is heterogeneous.)

questions.q: Why is the uncatalysed reaction between \(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{8}^{2-}}\) ions and \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) ions slow, and why do \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions speed it up?

options.A: Both reactants are negative ions that repel; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) gives two steps, each between oppositely charged ions.
options.B: Both reactants are negative ions that repel; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) adsorbs them onto its surface.
options.C: The reaction is endothermic; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) supplies the energy needed.
options.D: The ions are too large to collide; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) breaks them into smaller pieces.

questions.solution: Two negative ions repel, so the activation energy is high. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised by peroxodisulfate (\(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{8}^{2-} + 2Fe^{2+} \rightarrow 2SO_{4}^{2-} + 2Fe^{3+}}\)), then \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) oxidises iodide (\(\mathrm{2Fe^{3+} + 2I^{-} \rightarrow 2Fe^{2+} + I_{2}}\)). Each step is between oppositely charged ions, and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is regenerated. (It is in the same phase, so it has no surface.)

questions.q: How does the rate of reaction between acidified \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) ions and \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\) ions change as the reaction proceeds at constant temperature?

options.A: It is fastest at the start, then falls steadily as the reactants are used up.
options.B: It stays constant until one reactant runs out, then stops suddenly.
options.C: It is slow at first, then speeds up because the reaction is exothermic and warms the mixture.
options.D: It is slow at first, speeds up as \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ions form, then slows as the reactants are used up.

questions.solution: The product \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) catalyses the reaction (autocatalysis). At first there is almost no \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), so the reaction is slow; as it forms, the rate increases; finally the rate falls as \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\) are used up. (The temperature is constant, so warming is not the reason.)
